note: Party scorecards, post-WWII (calendar years 1948-2024, party of sitting president). Computation documented: annual averages by party-of-year from data/normalized/economic_indicators.json; S&P price returns from administration start/end index levels (Jan-Jan). CAUTION: sample = 37 Democratic years vs 40 Republican years; recessions cluster at Republican term starts (1969-70, 1973-75, 1981-82, 1990-91, 2001, 2007-09) and recoveries at Democratic starts — party attribution is contaminated by business-cycle timing. Do not read these as causal effects (root Sections 2, 10, 12).

real_gdp_growth.note: Wikipedia (quarterly annualized, 1947-2023): D ~4.6% vs R ~2.4% (gap ~1.8-2.2pp). Calendar-year computation here: D 3.6% vs R 2.7%. Gap shrinks when crisis-start years are excluded; direction robust.

unemployment.note: Direction robust (D lower), magnitude window-sensitive; some analyses (excluding 2009-11) show ~1-2pp gaps.

cpi_inflation.note: No robust party pattern. The 1970s inflation spanned Nixon/Ford (R) and Carter (D); 2021-22 spanned Biden (D). Post-1980: D 2.6% vs R 3.5% (driven by 1980s disinflation-era deficits under Reagan and low-inflation Obama years). Inflation is primarily a Fed/global phenomenon.

debt_gdp_public_change.unit: pp change in debt held by public / GDP over term
debt_gdp_public_change.note: Reagan +13, Bush41 +8, Clinton -14.5, Bush43 +20, Obama +24 (mostly crisis years 2009-11), Trump1 +23, Biden ~0 (flat as % of GDP). Both parties increased debt; only Clinton reduced it materially (1993 tax increase + growth + peace dividend).

democratic.note: Truman/Johnson/Clinton eras reduced debt/GDP via growth + surpluses

republican.note: Every GOP era since 1981 raised debt/GDP

sp500_price_return.note: D: Clinton +15.2, Obama +13.5, Biden +12.6 → avg ~13.8%. R: Reagan +13.3, Bush41 +10.5, Bush43 -6.2, Trump1 +13.3 → avg ~7.7%. Total-return studies (1928-2024): D ~14.8%/yr vs R ~9.3%/yr (median D 12.9% vs R 9.9%). Timing caveat: D terms began at crisis lows (2009, 2021) or after midterm corrections; dividends widen the D edge; concentration effects.

poverty_change.unit: pp change in official poverty rate over term
poverty_change.note: Big drops: Johnson (19.0→12.1), Clinton (15.1→11.3), early-2000s flat, Obama (12.5→12.7 net flat, trough 10.5 in 2019 post-term), Trump (12.3→11.4? COVID transfers lowered 2020 SPM; official 2020 11.4, 2021 11.6), Biden (11.6→11.1 2023, then 12.6 2024 as pandemic aid expired). D eras dominate the large reductions (1960s, 1990s, 2021 CTC experiment).
poverty_change.note2: Analyst judgment: the largest poverty reductions in modern history occurred under Democratic administrations via pro-poor transfer/tax policy; the 1996 welfare reform (bipartisan, signed by Clinton) is credited with caseload reduction but had contested deep-poverty effects.

life_expectancy_change.note: Long-run improvement ~0.15-0.25 yrs/yr through 2010 under both parties; stagnation 2011-2019 (deaths of despair) under Obama/Trump; COVID crash (2020-21) under Trump; recovery (2022-24) under Biden. Party differences are noise relative to the long-run trend and COVID shock.

freedom_indices_change.note: FH/V-Dem/EIU declines registered 2016-2026 across administrations of both parties (Trump 2017-2021: FH 94→83, V-Dem 0.79→0.72; Biden 2021-25: FH 83→83, V-Dem 0.72→0.75→0.57 in 2025; Trump II 2025-26: FH 83→81, V-Dem 0.75→0.57, EIU 7.85→7.65). The sharpest single-year declines (2025) occurred under Trump II; the 2016-2021 decline occurred under Trump I; longer-run erosion (money in politics, polarization, trust) is bipartisan and structural.

republican_edges: Inflation control post-1980 (completed via Volcker disinflation; Reagan-era policy acceptance of tight money)
Deregulation of transportation/energy (bipartisan origin; airline/trucking deregulation broadly judged welfare-positive)
Crime decline sustained through GOP eras (1990s-2010s — mostly state/local + demographics, not federal policy)
Cold War conclusion and defense posture (bipartisan, GOP-led)
Lower taxes on capital and business (their stated priority — delivered consistently)
democratic_edges: Higher average GDP growth and lower unemployment since WWII (timing-contaminated but robust in direction)
Stock market returns (robust in direction, timing-contaminated)
Poverty reduction via transfers and tax credits (1960s, 1990s, 2021 CTC)
Healthcare expansion (Medicare/Medicaid 1965, ACA 2010, IRA drug pricing 2022)
Fiscal consolidation when attempted (1993 deficit-reduction; 2010-15 deficit halving; Biden 2021-24 deficit reduction from crisis levels)
Financial regulation post-2008 (Dodd-Frank; bank capital; CFPB)
Civil rights and voting rights legislation (1964-65) and its enforcement legacy
bipartisan_failures: Federal debt accumulation since 1981 (R tax cuts + D spending + both parties' wars and crises)
Healthcare cost inflation (18% of GDP; both parties defended the system's rent-seeking while tinkering at the edges)
Housing affordability (both parties' land-use/subsidy/credit policies; NIMBY at local level)
Money in politics (Citizens United era; both parties benefit from and defend it)
Incarceration expansion 1980-2008 (both parties' crime politics; 1994 crime bill and 1980s-90s sentencing laws)
Opioid epidemic response (slow bipartisan reaction to prescription opioids; Purdue prosecutions late)
Financial deregulation pre-2008 (GLB 1999, CFMA 2000, GSE push, SEC 2004 — bipartisan)
Democracy erosion enablers (gerrymandering, primaries, polarization, executive power accumulation by both parties)
Tax complexity and corporate tax avoidance (both parties' loophole maintenance)
Failure to address entitlement solvency (Social Security/Medicare reform kicked down the road for 30+ years)
structural_factors_independent_of_party: Demographics: aging population → entitlement spending growth and slower potential growth
Healthcare cost growth is the single largest fiscal driver (system structure, not one party)
Technology and automation (labor share of income fell 2000-2015)
Globalization and import competition (manufacturing employment decline)
Financialization and rising asset values (Fed policy + global savings glut)
Interest-rate normalization after 2021 (debt burden rise is mechanical)
